title: Origen and Alexandria
hook: a brilliant teacher who read scripture on many levels; some of his ideas were later rejected

segments.voice: Yesterday, Perpetua and Felicity, and their passio. Your line was sisters in the arena.

A father in Alexandria makes his son learn a passage of scripture every day. The boy, Origen, isn't satisfied with the plain words. He keeps asking: but what does it mean, underneath? Eusebius says his father scolded him for asking questions beyond his years, and was secretly delighted. Then persecution comes, and the father is arrested. The boy wants to go and die with him, and his mother, out of options, hides all his clothes so he can't leave the house. He writes his father a letter instead.
screen: `A PASSAGE EVERY DAY.` → `WHAT DOES IT MEAN, UNDERNEATH?` → `HIS MOTHER HID HIS CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: Origen grew up to teach in Alexandria, in Egypt, and Eusebius says he was put in charge of instructing people preparing for baptism. He never stopped asking the boy's question. First, his picture. In On First Principles, Origen says scripture is like a human being, with a body, a soul and a spirit. The body is the plain sense: the story, what happened, what the words say. The soul is what the passage asks of the way you live. The spirit is what it shows about Christ and the life to come. Second, the Church kept the layers. The Catechism of the Catholic Church still speaks of the literal sense of scripture and the spiritual senses built on it, and insists the spiritual senses rest on the literal one. Its example: the crossing of the Red Sea is a real escape from Egypt, and it's also read as a sign of Christ's victory and of baptism. Third, the caution. Origen was a bold thinker, and some of his guesses were later judged to go too far. The Church rejected certain ideas linked with his name, like souls existing before their bodies. He isn't honored as a saint. Fourth, why it matters. A verse can be read once, closed and filed. Or it can be read again and again and give something new each time, the way a friend of many years can still surprise you. Origen read that way all his life, starting as a boy who wanted to know what was underneath.
screen: `BODY, SOUL AND SPIRIT.` · `THE LITERAL SENSE COMES FIRST.` · `SOME IDEAS WENT TOO FAR.` · `READ IT AGAIN.` · then, large: `LAYERS OF MEANING.`

segments.voice: Here's a line from the psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "The Lord ruleth me: and I shall want nothing." Read it plainly first: someone in charge, someone looked after, nobody going without, and the next verse sets the scene in a place of pasture and water. Then say it again slowly and let it ask about your own life: what do you want today that you might not need, and where are you being led? If you pray, say the line once more as a prayer.
Origen. The teacher in Alexandria who read scripture in layers, body, soul and spirit, beginning as a boy who asked what lay underneath. Today's word.
Your line: layers of meaning. The plain sense first, then the rest. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching distinguishes the literal sense of scripture from its spiritual senses, and the practice of lectio divina reads a short passage slowly, more than once, letting it speak in layers.

notes: Eusebius HE 6.2 paraphrased: Leonides had Origen learn scripture daily; the boy sought deeper meanings; his father rebuked him outwardly and rejoiced inwardly; during persecution the mother hid his clothes; he wrote urging his father not to change his mind on the family's account; the father was martyred. HE 6.3: Origen put in charge of catechetical instruction. Confirm.

On First Principles 4.2.4 (body, soul, spirit of scripture, as in a human being) paraphrased; the script's glosses of soul (how you live) and spirit (Christ and the life to come) are simplifications. Confirm.
CCC 115–117: literal and spiritual senses (allegorical, moral, anagogical); all senses founded on the literal; Red Sea crossing as sign of Christ's victory and of baptism. Confirm.

'Later, Church councils rejected certain ideas linked with his name, like souls existing before their bodies': the anathemas associated with the Second Council of Constantinople and the Edict of Justinian; a scholar should confirm the wording and whether 'councils' (plural) is fair. No dates given.
'He isn't honored as a saint' and 'Catholic writers still quote him with care': confirm phrasing.
Douay-Rheims Psalm 22:1 'The Lord ruleth me: and I shall want nothing.': confirm exact punctuation.
